channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette
channel.description: Your premier source for satirical news from across the realms. All the news that's fit to print (or burn).

item.title: Rust Monster Asleep on Level Seven Steps, Guild Sells Tickets
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: Chapter 9 is charging admission to watch a rust monster nap on Level Seven's top step, and the Fourth Attempt has left its armor at home.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 6 — The rust monster that ate the Level Seven ribbon-cutting shears is still asleep on the top step, and Chapter 9 has started charging four silver to look at it. I paid. It is a very large, very round animal, and it snores like a portcullis.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick, Chapter 9's spokesman, calls the arrangement "a soft launch of Level Seven." Tickets include a lantern rental, a laminated map, and a waiver against loss of metal. "The level is not open," he told me, "but it is on track, and the monster is part of the track." He then asked me to hold a door. I declined. I always decline.

The trouble is the stairs. Nobody can get past the rust monster without waking it, and nobody can wake it without losing everything iron they own. The Fourth Attempt arrived this morning in boiled leather, a wooden shield, and a sling. Box score: fighter 31 hit points of 38, cleric 22 of 22, wizard 9 of 14, and one hireling holding a spoon carved from a table leg. Their bard, who asked to be named, said the party felt "lighter, and a bit foolish." He did not give his name. Nobody has ever heard it.

The party got within six steps before the monster sneezed. The sling bullets, being lead, were not a problem. The wizard's belt buckle was. He is now holding his trousers up with a ferret, which he says is "temporary."

Ansel Pottage, steward of the Fourth Attempt's hirelings, read the waiver to the end, which is more than the party did. "Clause nine says the guild is not responsible for armor, weapons, buckles, hinges, or 'personal ironwork,'" he said. "I would like it noted that I own a pair of spectacles." He is owed a new pair, he says, and the claim is in.

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society has refused it. A spokesman said rust monster damage is covered only if the policyholder "did not walk up to the rust monster." Reeve Maudrey Fennick, whose ceremonial chain was among the first casualties, appeared in a replacement made of braided rope and a single brass bell. "We are aware of the monster," she said. "We are aware of the bell." She has asked Chapter 9 to put the ticket money toward a way around the creature, such as a second stair. Oddingwick says a second stair "is on the list."

Ten-foot pole count this season: seven. The seventh went to the monster, which ate it in one bite and looked, I thought, pleased with the effort. I rolled poorly on that one. I held it too close.

Chapter 9 says the level is mostly cleared. The step has a rust monster on it. Mostly is doing a lot of work.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Copper Thief Dives Through Window, Leaves His ID in Backpack
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A copper thief fled a deputy by diving through a closed window, then left his backpack and driver's license behind. The Watch is allegedly thrilled.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the third bell after midnight on the first of the month, a deputy of the Oakahoma County Sheriff's Watch was allegedly called to an empty house where a copper thief was allegedly stripping the walls. The thief ran, dove headfirst through a closed window, and vanished. The Watch released the scrying-lens footage this week, and the whole county has watched it eleven times.

The footage is magnificent. The deputy says "Hey!" The thief, mid-pipe, says nothing, because he is already airborne. Glass goes everywhere. Allegedly he did not slow down, and allegedly he did not look back. A bystander named Dolly Quickfinger, who was eating a pickled egg on the porch across the road at the time, said, "I've seen a lot of windows. That one was the fastest window I ever saw lose."

The deputy searched the area with a patrol wagon and a floating observer-eye, both of which found nothing. The thief was gone with his pockets full of copper: wiring, pipe, the innards of an old stove. Not a gold piece in the haul. A hundred coppers make a gold piece, so by my math he risked his face for roughly one decent dinner.

Here is where it gets good. He left his bicycle behind. He left his backpack behind. In the backpack, per the Sheriff's Watch, was his driver's license. Name, face, and home address, all printed neatly on a card he apparently carries to burglaries. The Watch called this "a significant investigative aid." I call it leaving a calling card, and not a fancy one.

He is charged with burglary, resisting arrest, and obstructing an officer, and he has a prior record in the county for theft, drug offenses, and an assault charge. As of the latest reports he is still at large. Allegedly.

Ooh, wait. There is a really nice brass lantern in the evidence photo. Look at the hinges on that thing. Anyway. Sheriff's Watch spokespeople asked anyone with information to come forward, and also asked residents to stop asking whether the window was "okay." Windows, they said, are not witnesses.

Neighbors in the Lower Fields say the old house has been picked clean for a month. "Somebody has to do it, I suppose," said Hobb Tanglebrook, a hay-cart mender. "They just shouldn't use the glass as a door." The Watch agrees on both counts.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Sea Ice Hits Record-Low Winter Peak; Frost Giants Evicted
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: Sea ice on the Sea of Moving Ice is thinner and younger, says the Astral Navy, and Brother Wendell prescribes soup for the melting.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, the sea ice is melting again. The Astral Navy reports that winter sea ice on the Sea of Moving Ice tied last year's record-low peak in March, and the September minimum, reached on the twelfth, came in at 1.78 million square miles. That ties three earlier years for the tenth-lowest in about fifty years of scrying-crystal records.

The Navy's polar clerks say what is left is thinner and younger. Old, thick, multiyear ice has declined a great deal, and the thin first-year stuff now does most of the work. I think of it as an infirmary staffed entirely by apprentices. They mean well. They also melt.

Now, the old herbals say nothing about ice, but they do say that a thing cannot be rushed, and a floe that has taken years to thicken does not come back in one cold season. The actual study is the satellite record itself, and it is plain enough. Every summer from 2007 through this one ranks among the twenty lowest on the books. The lowest of all was 2012, which the clerks still discuss the way old soldiers discuss a bad winter campaign.

There is one small mercy. Summer losses have slowed lately, and the clerks say short-term weather can swing the numbers a great deal. I am glad to hear it. I am less glad to hear the fine print, which is that the Sea of Moving Ice could be free of summer ice at least once before the middle of the century. A slow leak is still a leak, friends.

Consider the animals, because I always do. The white bears, the walrus herds, and the seals who raise their pups on that ice have no say in the quarterly reports of any guild. The frost giants who rent the northern floes have already begun filing eviction complaints against the weather. Meanwhile the fire elementals in the great foundries keep chugging along, and nobody asks the seals if they mind. I mind. I mind quite a lot.

The Navy's clerks, to their credit, keep measuring and keep publishing, which is more than can be said for certain potion-makers I will not name. Honest counting is a kind of herbalism. You write down what the plant did, not what you hoped it would do.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil says there is an app that tracks the ice live. Go outside, Nyx, and look at a puddle. For everyone else, this week calls for a pot of hot barley, parsnip, and smoked-trout chowder, thick enough to stand a spoon in, since someone ought to keep things thick.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Red-Carpet State Visit Leaves Red Oliphants Fuming
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: Senators in the Party of the Red Oliphant blast Donwald's cannon-salute state visit for Emperor Shi, a parley heavy on pageantry and light on results.
item.content:encoded:
Councilors of the Party of the Red Oliphant spent the week angry at their own High Lord over a state visit. High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers rolled out a hundred-foot red carpet, a cannon salute and an honor guard for Celestial Emperor Shi of Kara-Tur. Weeks later, the red carpet is still the only thing anyone can show for it.

I have covered nineteen sieges. This was the first where the host brought the battering ram a bouquet.

The Emperor landed at the Royal Landing Field of Andrewhold. Donwald met him at the foot of the carpet. Handshake: firm, two seconds, no hidden dagger detected. Which is the problem. The dagger was apparently elsewhere. Councilors learned in a closed-door briefing that Kara-Tur was likely deepening its military ties to Calimshan. They also heard that Calimshan's clerics had used Kara-Tur's eyes-in-the-sky imagery to target Waterdeep's garrisons abroad. Donwald gave the Emperor a tour of the Golden Tower's building projects and a stroll past his Walk of Fame.

Councilor Wicker-Mist, chair of the Chamber's war committee, rose on the floor and said he would have advised against the invitation. Councilor Thornis, retiring and thus free of fear, called the welcome a "what-the-hell moment" and noted the Emperor got a bigger carpet than Duke Volodar of Vaasa ever did. Even the loud scribes of the Oliphant fringe joined in. Rare. Like a dragon agreeing with a knight.

The Golden Tower's reply: the Emperor hosted Donwald in Kara-Tur earlier this year, so the favor was owed. Fair. Armies repay hospitality too, usually with fire.

What did the parley produce? A shared view that the oil strait should stay open, which was already everyone's view. Some trade-ledger chatter. A banquet. No grand bargain on the tariffs, on the arcane engines, on the Eastern Isle, or on the seven-month war with Calimshan that the High Lord is holding off until the ballots are counted. The Blue Donkeys called it pageantry over substance. They are correct, and it costs them nothing to say so.

Tension between the Chamber and the Golden Tower now holds at roughly twelve siege-days. Tension between the Golden Tower and Calimshan holds at about two hundred. Donwald appears to be negotiating with the wrong one of them.

The Emperor went home with his carpet burns and his satellites. Nobody won. Somebody will lose tomorrow, and I suspect it is whoever has troops standing under those satellites.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: New Tablets Start at 230 gp; Echo Slate Runs on Rival's OS
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Amazoom's new Echo Slate tablets start at 230 gp, run Gargoogle's bazaar, and read your screen. Nyx tested all three. Byte has notes.
item.content:encoded:
Amazoom Caravans has launched a new line of tablets, and I have had all three on my workbench since Wednesday! The Echo Slate 12 Pro, the Echo Slate 11 and the Echo Slate 8 start at 500, 330 and 230 gp, and they went on sale in Waterdeep on the 14th. Every single one is a tablet that finally talks back, and I mean that in the most excited way possible.

First, the big news: these are not another sealed-garden slate. The old Ember tablets are gone, replaced by a clean-sheet design that runs a droid-golem operating system and opens Gargoogle's Bazaar on day one. Amazoom insists this is a brand-new line and not an Ember in a trench coat. I held an Echo Slate next to my last Ember and the trench coat hypothesis is very much alive.

The hardware is gorgeous! The 12 Pro has a 12-inch crystal pane, a 120-beat refresh glyph and a body only six and a half millimeters thick, with an optional anti-glare Nanomatte pane for 550 gp. Amazoom claims nearly triple the mana throughput of the old models and nine times the graphics. I can confirm that my scrying-hockey game now renders the goalie's regret in real time. The 11 comes in Amethyst and Matcha. The 8 weighs 329 grams and comes in aluminum, which is great, because I threw it at a door later and the door lost.

Now the headline feature: Echo Stones Plus lives inside every Slate. Hold the Ask button and the Stone answers from any app. Its On-Screen Intelligence reads whatever is on your display and offers advice, such as picking the best hiking trail from a list of trails. It is off until you opt in, which is a very polite way to say it wants to look at your screen. Byte, my pseudodragon familiar, caught a glimpse of the setup menu and said, "Your data is our treasure. Try Echo Plus today."

There is also a new Kindlingscroll reading mode that silences notifications, dims the blue light and promises twenty hours of battery. I read one chapter. A Stone politely suggested a different chapter. Then it suggested a sequel. Then it asked whether I would like to be reminded about the sequel's sequel. The runic latency on that upsell is world-class.

Kid-proof editions of the 8 and 11 ship in padded cases with a year of the Kids' Menagerie subscription, which is the one part I hate. A year of subscription means a second year of subscription, and I will be waiting for that invoice with my eyebrows crossed.

Verdict: Four and a half out of five beholder eyes. The half-eye was deducted because the 12 Pro's optional Pro Keyboard bit me. It was affectionate, probably.

Damage Report: Burns sustained: 1. Doors defeated: 1. Eyebrows: pending. Subscriptions accidentally joined: 2.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

item.title: Teachers Strike Vote in Lindenwick: First in 50 Years
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Lindenwick teachers authorized a strike for the first time in nearly 50 years after turning down a 3 percent raise. Brakka did the arithmetic.
item.content:encoded:
Teachers in the Evergreen Reach just held a teachers strike vote and authorized a walkout, the first in nearly fifty years. They will walk out on the 28th unless somebody finds a better offer.

Here is the setup. The Lindenwick Educators' Guild, which speaks for the teachers of the Lindenwick Schoolhouse District, met Tuesday. More than a hundred of them rejected the district's latest offer and voted to strike. They have worked without a contract since term began. Talks started seven months ago. Seven months is long enough to grow a child, and it has not produced a contract.

The offer is a 3 percent raise for the year: 2.6 for the cost of living plus 0.4 for good measure. That means a pay cut with a ribbon on it.

"We are not asking to be rich," said Brindle Oakenshaw, a tutor of arithmetic for fourteen years and one of the Guild's stewards. "We are asking for planning time. A teacher who plans nothing is a teacher improvising in front of thirty children, and some of us have seen how that ends." The Guild also wants more help for the schoolhouse's counselors and mind-healers, and a say in how late-arrival time gets spent. The Guild's president asked for "respect for our time and professional judgment." Fair. That is cheap, and it still hasn't been offered.

The district's superintendent says there is no money. He points to about a million gold pieces lost as enrollment fell, a liability-insurance bill up 84.4 percent in four years, and a 1.1-million-gold-piece hole from the Margrave's underfunding of special schooling. Voters also turned down three bond measures and a levy. "Valuing our employees and protecting the long-term financial health of the district are not opposing responsibilities," he said. Nice sentence. That means no.

The district also notes that teacher pay rose nearly 25 percent over three years and that the average salary last year was 114,711 gold pieces. I have heard that figure before, from guildmasters, usually right before they cut something. An average is how a district buries its worst-paid under its best-paid. Ask the new hire at the bottom of the scale what she earns, then ask what her rent is.

Lindenwick is not a hotbed. The last school walkout nearby was a couple of years back, when the classroom helpers in the next town put down their chalk. Before that you have to go back close to half a century. These are not troublemakers. These are people who color-code their calendars. When they walk out, something has gone badly wrong at the table.

It is the same story Corvallow's town workers told this week: the budget has a hole, the workers are standing next to it, and somehow the hole is their fault. Bargaining resumes Monday at nine in the morning. Bring the money. Bring a lunch break too.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Bank Earnings: Goldmane Equities Trading Up 72%
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Bank earnings beat forecasts as Goldmane's equities trading jumps 72%. Sterling Vanmoor calls the 450 million gp charity gift a brand pivot.
item.content:encoded:
The counting houses of the Merchant Princes just posted third-quarter bank earnings, and the numbers are the kind I frame and hang above my sword rack. Goldmane Sacks reported 18.68 billion gp in revenue, with its equities trading desk up 72 percent from last year. Analysts had predicted 17.03 billion gp. They were, if I may say so, thinking too small.

Let me break down the winners. Guildmaster Dravid Solomancer of Goldmane credited the result to clients who "continued to turn to Goldmane for world-class advice, execution and financing." That is thought-leading language. Advisory fees hit a record 1.65 billion gp as merger volume climbed, and I have rarely been prouder of a stack of merging guilds. Assets under supervision reached 4.1 trillion gp. That is a dragon hoard with a compliance department.

Some skeptics will point to the footnotes. The pipeline of future advisory deals shrank. The firm's capital cushion slid from 14.3 to 12.4 percent. And roughly 450 million gp went to its charitable fund, which dented profit. I prefer to call that a brand pivot toward goodwill. Goodwill, for the unfamiliar, is the only asset a guild can print on demand.

Over at Jaypee Morgrim Chasehold, quarterly profit came in at 15.3 billion gp, about 5.57 gp a share. Some bean-counters wanted 5.93. The stock barely moved, which I call a "stability-forward growth posture." Meanwhile Wellspring Fargate took in 21.87 billion gp and its shares slid 3 percent. I'd describe that as "rightsizing the adventuring party's expectations."

I met Guildmaster Solomancer once, at a charity auction in a hall that smelled of old money and mulled wine. He looked at my business card, handed it to a servant, and said, "Keep hustling, young man." I have not stopped hustling since. I have also not been invited back, but that's just the market giving me room to scale. If you want to see how the rest of the Merchant Princes are celebrating, my colleague covered the coin piles hitting record heights, though he seemed gloomy about it. Unions and regulators will always find a cloud around a gold lining. I find the lining.

Goldmane also bought back 2.9 million of its own shares at about 1,049 gp each. A guild that buys itself is a guild that believes in itself. Also, it signed two new acquisitions, because a Q3 without a merger is just a long weekend.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • When your trading desk is up 72 percent, a 450 million gp donation is just a very large networking event.
  • A thinner deal pipeline is only a pipeline that is being gently curated.
  • Always bring a business card, even if it ends up with the servants.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Midterm Ad Spending Tops 10 Billion Gold Pieces, Loaves Wept
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: Midterm campaign ad spending has passed 10 billion gp, or 166 billion loaves. Barnaby has checked the math. He is not well.
item.content:encoded:
Campaign ad spending for the coming midterm elections has passed 10 billion gp, according to the Ad-Imp Augury Bureau, which tracks every ad the Red Oliphants and Blue Donkeys buy and sells the numbers back to them. The Bureau says the total will keep climbing until Election Day, just under three weeks away.

Ten billion gp is a number I cannot hold in my head, so I held it in loaves. On the Loaf Index, where one honest loaf is 6 copper, that is about 166 billion loaves. (I have checked this four times. I did it again just now. Still 166 billion.) That is a staggering amount of bread, and instead of being eaten it is being spent to tell people a Councilor once voted for something.

The Bureau's figures are specific, so I will be too. The Red Oliphants are outspending the Blue Donkeys by about 11 percent, a gap of roughly 133 million gp. That is 2.2 billion loaves. The Chamber Leadership Hoard, the Oliphants' war chest for Senate Chamber races, is on pace for 310 million gp on its own, or 5.2 billion loaves. Add its six affiliated war chests and the whole network reaches about 643 million gp. I stopped converting at that point because my pencil snapped.

The costliest single contest is in the Lone Star Marches, where about 500 million gp of ads are scheduled, driven by long primaries and a runoff. That is 8.3 billion loaves for one seat. In the Golden Coast, the race for governor is projected at 346 million gp. A Coinlord there spent roughly 210 million gp of his own money on ads and still lost his primary in the summer. I want to be fair to him: 210 million gp is 35 billion loaves, and nobody has ever lost a bread-eating contest that big.

Here is the economics underneath the joke. Ad spending is not coin vanishing into a hole. It lands as revenue for scroll-printers, crier guilds and the scrying-glass networks that carry the ads, which is partly why those businesses love an election year. But the Bureau's count leaves out hundreds of millions in other political spending, and late ad buys are still arriving. The real total will be higher. When something is certain to be larger than the number printed, I tend to lie down.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, received eleven ad scrolls and four crier visits about the Chamber races this week. She says she has never been so well informed and so unable to vote for anyone. She also says the boot is looking better and better. I used to laugh at her.

What this means for your pantry: the ads will end on Election Day, but the flour will not get cheaper. Buy a sack before the next speech.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Donwald's Sanctions Waiver Spares Damara Oil Tariffs
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A sanctions waiver freed Damara from oil tariffs a day before they started, and Councilors of both parties are furious but in recess.
item.content:encoded:
High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers signed a decree late Friday waiving the sanctions law, the Grimm Damaran Sanctions Act, one day before most of it was due to take effect. The Act placed steep tariffs on any realm buying Damaran oil and fuel. The Senate Chamber passed it 86 to 11, and Donwald signed it himself about a month ago.

Procedure is my religion, so allow me to explain. A sanctions waiver is the part of a law that lets the Seat decline to enforce it "for reasons of national security." The decree gives no end date and gives the reason in one sentence. The reason, as far as the gallery can tell, is a diesel arrangement with Czar Vlad the Bear-Handed. Donwald says the deal will lower fuel prices at home. Earlier this month Donwald also announced an "energy ceasefire" that Vaasa says Damara ignored. Promises Made: two. Promises Kept: a waiver.

The gentleman from the Carolan Reach, Councilor Thornis, a member of Donwald's own Red Oliphant party, called the decree "beyond irresponsible." He asked what part of enforcing a law passed 86 to 11 the Keep fails to understand. I have read the Act. It is eleven pages, and I can report that no part of it is confusing, which is rare for a document produced by this Chamber.

The lady from Mastiffchusetts, Councilor Elizabeth Warrant, said Donwald was "thumbing his nose" at the Council. Grand Vizier Chuck Schemer said the diesel dealings "keep getting dirtier," which is accurate and was, I assume, intended as a pun. Duke Volodar of Vaasa said he hoped the sanctions could be revived. He may be the only person in the matter who has stated a hope and not a position.

Several Councilors have promised a response. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me what that response will be. The Senate Chamber and the Chamber of Commons are both in recess until after the elections. Representative Gregory Meekes of the Chamber of Commons has filed a bill to block the diesel deal. It cannot be voted on until the Chambers reconvene, and by then the fuel will have been delivered and burned.

The waiver is already in force. The Council's two chambers may overturn it only with a vote, and they are not in town to hold one. The motion to recess carried. Nobody objected.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Starfinder Tech Core Adds Tactical Starship Combat
item.dc:creator: Matthias Ashmoor
item.description: Paizo's Starfinder Tech Core is out: a 264-page, $69.99 hardcover for Starfinder Second Edition with starship combat and two new classes.
item.content:encoded:
AT THE ASHFORGE — Starfinder Tech Core, the newest rulebook for Paizo's Starfinder Second Edition, went on sale October 7. It's a 264-page hardcover at $69.99, per Paizo's store listing, and its headline feature is tactical starship combat. It also adds two classes, the mechanic and the technomancer. A book whose contents page reads like a parts list has my full attention.

How the ship fights

Starship combat, in chapter 6, runs on two maps at once, lead designer Dustin Knight explained on the Paizo blog. Characters move around a battle map of their own ship and spend their three actions a turn helming a station, repairing damaged areas, bolstering allies, or handling enemies and hazards that turn up aboard. A separate sensor map tracks the distance between ships. There the pilot can Boost Thrusters, Change Heading, or Juke to leave enemy ships open to the gunners.

Each class gets a job. Soldiers fire starship-scale weapons with their own proficiencies and feats and can hit several enemies with Area Fire. Operatives use Aim to deal extra damage to a single ship. Drone pilots plant mines or block incoming attacks, and spellcasters channel spells through the ship's magic conduit. Every battle station has upgrade slots, and Knight's examples include deploying a turret, installing mines into a drone, and turning the ship's prow into a solar weapon for ramming. I once bolted a ram onto a siege cart, but it never ran on a sun. I'm taking notes.

Ships can also take expansion bays such as a medbay or a holoden, plus upgraded escape pods, and the chapter gives guidance for introducing, upgrading, and running starships across a campaign.

The order slip

  • Released: October 7, 2026 (per The Gaming Gang)
  • Price: $69.99 hardcover; Paizo also lists Pocket, Sketch, and Special Editions, and a limited Retailer Edition with a retro game-box cover
  • Pages: 264
  • Classes: mechanic and technomancer
  • Archetypes: nanocyte and junkomancer
  • Ancestries and heritages: robotic SROs, living holograms, and cyborgs
  • Also inside: tech companions, technology feats, armor, weapons, augmentations, magic items, high-tech spells, and sample starship foes and hazards
  • Credits: designed by Jessica Catalan, Dustin Knight, and Aras Yazgan, developed by Jenny Jarzabski and Mike Kimmel, per Angus Abranson's PDF spotlight

The PDF is on DriveThruRPG, Abranson notes. For the record, a junkomancer is the closest thing the far plane has printed to my job description, and I'd like royalties.

— M.A., from the forge

item.title: Wizards of the Coast Declines to Recognize D&D Union
item.dc:creator: Matthias Ashmoor
item.description: Wizards of the Coast won't voluntarily recognize the D&D and Studio X union, sending it to an NLRB secret-ballot vote. No date is set yet.
item.content:encoded:
AT THE ASHFORGE — Wizards of the Coast will not voluntarily recognize the union formed by its Dungeons & Dragons team and Studio X, so the question goes to a secret-ballot election run by the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB). The workers had asked for recognition by October 13. On October 14 the union, United Wizards of the Coast-CWA, posted that the company had declined, and a Wizards spokesperson confirmed it to Wargamer. No vote date has been set.

The whole workforce at the Ashforge is me, the bellows, and an apprentice who mostly sweeps, so I'll leave labor law to the far plane and report what each side has said.

The D&D unit includes D&D Beyond staff, per Dungeons & Dragons Fan. Wargamer describes Studio X as the group that covers most of the creative staff on Magic: The Gathering. Both teams announced on October 6 that they would join United Wizards of the Coast, which is affiliated with the Communication Workers of America. That union formed in June after the MTG Arena development team voted 83% in favor. Wizards did not voluntarily recognize that unit either, Wargamer reports.

What Wizards says

In an internal email to US staff, Wizards' leadership wrote that "we are best able to keep building great games and a great place to work by working directly with employees" and that "Wizards is not neutral on the question of unionization," Dungeons & Dragons Fan reports. The same email said, "in the end, we will respect the results of the election, no matter what our employees choose." It also listed average base salary for individual contributors up 20% since 2023, 2025 bonuses reaching 200% of target, five weeks of paid time off, subsidized medical benefits, and free product.

What the union says

The union is campaigning for fair wages and career progression, job security, remote work protections and sustainable workloads, affordable healthcare, an enforceable AI policy, and ownership of what employees make in their own time, which Wizards currently claims under its IP terms. "We know the workers that make the game can and should be treated better, and our aim is to show that to the world through our union efforts," the D&D team wrote in its October 6 letter, Rascal reported. The organizers say they have "a public supermajority of employees committed to our cause."

What's next

The NLRB will hold a secret-ballot vote of staff in both units. Bell of Lost Souls expects voting as soon as next month; Dungeons & Dragons Fan puts it within several months. Either way, the result will decide whether the people who make D&D and Magic bargain with Wizards as a union.

— M.A., from the forge

item.title: Paizo's 13 Omens Horror RPG Launches on Kickstarter
item.dc:creator: Matthias Ashmoor
item.description: Paizo's rules-lite horror RPG 13 Omens raised $235,084 from 1,702 backers in its first day on Kickstarter. It closes Friday, November 13.
item.content:encoded:
AT THE ASHFORGE — 13 Omens, a rules-lite supernatural horror RPG from Paizo, the publisher of Pathfinder and Starfinder, is live on Kickstarter. The campaign launched October 14 and had raised $235,084 from 1,702 backers by the next morning, ICv2 reports. It closes on Friday, November 13. That is either very good marketing or a very bad sign, and I've hung a horseshoe over the forge door to be safe.

Jason Bulmahn, the lead designer of the original Pathfinder Roleplaying Game, designed it with Joe Pasini, per Tabletop Sentinel, and James Jacobs led narrative development, according to Paizo's blog. The d20 stays home this time; 13 Omens runs on six-siders. Every session is a one-shot with a prologue and three acts that build to a horror-movie climax. One player is the Host, and Paizo recommends four or five others around the table.

The bag of bad luck

The hook is a shared, opaque dice bag. On a check, a player draws two d6s and tries to meet a target number, TTRPG Fans explains. The bag starts with eight Safe dice and one Omen die, and the Host adds more Omen dice from a reserve of 13 as the acts go on. An Omen die that rolls at or below the current act number deals a Wound. The Host never rolls at all. Three Wounds bring a permanent Flaw, and a fourth means death or removal from play. Each character can Cheat Death once per story, or make a Valiant Sacrifice: an automatic success that costs their life.

I reach into a bin of rivets without looking a hundred times a day. Most of what comes out is fine. The far tables are about to find out what happens when it isn't.

The order slip

  • PDF rulebook: $15
  • Physical rulebook: $35
  • Standard physical bundle: $120
  • Top tiers: an online game with one of the designers at $2,500, an in-person game at next year's Gen Con at $5,000, and an "Executive Producer" credit at $10,000, per EN World
  • Dice kit: 21 dice (8 Safe, 13 Omen) and the bag, with a special set made from elk bone (Tabletop Sentinel)
  • Retail release: June 2, 2027 (ICv2)

Paizo will add a retailer tier on October 21 so game stores can preorder the core book, GM screen, and dice, ICv2 reports. EN World says the campaign cleared $150,000 on its first day, and its coverage links a free demo for anyone who wants to shake the bag before pledging. The add-ons also include cards, tokens, plushies, satchels, and skulls, for those who like their dread with merchandise.

— M.A., from the forge

item.title: Mimic Hearing Ends When Witness Chair Eats Exhibit A
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: Chapter 9 ruled a mimic is a monster for hazard pay after the adventuring party's witness chair bit the examiner. The hirelings of the Fourth Attempt win.
item.content:encoded:
BRINDLEMOOR, CHAPTER 9 HEARING ROOM, 0 FEET UNDERGROUND (still checking) — Chapter 9 ruled this morning that a mimic is a monster for the purposes of hazard pay, ending the grievance filed by the hirelings of the Fourth Attempt. The ruling came about four minutes after the witness chair bit the hearing examiner.

The hearing opened on time, which Chapter 9 staff called "unprecedented" and a few called "suspicious." Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor sat at the bench. Ansel Pottage, steward of the hirelings, stood at the lectern with the contract that listed a mimic as furniture, one thumb still in a bandage. The party's bard, who asked to be named, sat in the gallery on what he described as "a very welcoming stool."

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick argued for the guild. Schedule C, he said, covers "miscellaneous furnishings," and a mimic is miscellaneous by nature. Pottage replied that the chest, the stool, and now apparently the witness chair were all in the same room, and asked the examiner to count how many of them had teeth. Oddingwick called this "a leading question about furniture."

The turn came when Brackenmoor asked the mimic, which had been invited and was seated as the witness chair, to state its name for the record. It did not. It closed on her sleeve. She was freed in two minutes by the court usher and a ladle. Her hit points went from 13 to 9, a box score the hearing room's scribe entered in the minutes with visible pleasure.

"The witness has demonstrated its character," Brackenmoor said, rubbing her arm. "Furniture does not do that. A mule might. A mule is a beast and gets hazard pay. I find the mimic is a monster whenever it bites, and I will take no further questions on the stool."

The ruling backdates hazard pay to the first bite and adds one clause: anyone calling a thing "just a chest" must open it first, at their own expense. Pottage called it "fair, and read aloud, which is all I ever ask." Asked about the replacement thumb, he said the guild had "taken it under advisement." Oddingwick said the outcome was a "soft launch of the monster framework" and that Chapter 9 remained "on track."

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society, which had hoped to avoid choosing a claim form, chose the monster form. "It's longer," an adjuster said. "But it has a box for thumbs."

The stool in question has still not been identified as a mimic. It has been taken into Chapter 9's custody and is, for now, being held in the evidence room. The cook who was sitting on it declined to comment. The mimic itself left the building as a bench in the lobby, where it has already bitten two petitioners waiting on permits. Reeve Maudrey Fennick has been asked to rule on whether lobby seating is a monster. She said, "We are aware of the bench."

Ten-foot pole count for the season: eight. The eighth was lost to the lobby bench, which I should have known. I rolled poorly.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: 10 Live Birds in His Smalls: Skyport Wardens Cry Fowl
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A traveler allegedly hid 10 live birds in pockets sewn into his underwear at Mirage Bay Skyport. Wardens call it smuggling. Skritch calls it a scoop.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell past noon, a traveler stepping off an airship from the Nelanther Isles was allegedly stopped at Mirage Bay Skyport with a bulge near his waist and ten live birds hidden in his underwear. The Gatewardens say pockets had been sewn into the garment, and each pocket allegedly held a small plastic tub of bird. A smuggling charge followed.

The traveler, a lawful resident of Waterdeep, allegedly told wardens the birds were "for personal use." Wardens did not ask which personal. He had allegedly written "No" on his customs scroll beside the question about animals, which is technically a statement about the man and not the birds. He was released on a bond of 25,000 gp. The birds, I am told, are fine, and are now in the custody of people with a proper aviary.

I reached the scene by sewer grate, as is my right. "I thought he was just happy to be home," said Tobbin Fenwick, a porter who was eating a pickled egg at the time. "Then something in there went cheep. I put the egg down. I never put the egg down." Fenwick has since finished the egg, allegedly.

The Gatewardens, who answer to the Homeland Watchtower, would not say what kind of birds they were, which is how you know it was a scoop. Rumor at the scanner desk says a customs hound sat down and stared at the man's belt for a full minute, wagging, with the look of a hound who has found the best day of his career.

Look, I have covered the Lower City docks for years and I have seen contraband in barrels, in boots, and once in a very patient cow. Never in the smalls. That takes planning. That takes a needle. Also, somebody at the skyport dropped a silver button near gate nine, and it is gorgeous. Anyway.

The Watchtower reminds all travelers that live birds, like live anything, must be declared on the scroll, and that "personal use" is not a recognized customs category. The Tower District nobles, naturally, say nothing about this, because they smuggle by the crate and call it "imports." Pigeons could not be reached for comment, because I did not look for them.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Eye Redness Drops Go Nonprescription; Beholders Squint
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: The Potion & Provisions Authority cleared a nonprescription eye drop for redness, and Brother Wendell would like everyone to sleep first.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, the Potion & Provisions Authority has approved the first nonprescription eye drop of its kind for eye redness, a little vial called Brightlid Eye-Dew from Alchon Optical Alchemists. It is cleared for anyone twelve and older, and it is the same medicine, in a gentler dose, that the glaucoma clinics have long kept behind the counter.

Now, the old herbals say a red eye wants rest, a cool cloth of chamomile tea, and a good long cry about nothing in particular. The Authority's own label says much the same thing in smaller letters: no more than twice a day, take out your contact crystals first, wait ten minutes before putting them back, and wait five minutes between different drops. If the redness lasts past three days, or your eye hurts, or your vision goes strange, stop and see a cleric. That is not marketing copy. That is the whole instruction manual, and it is sensible.

Mikel Davros, Director of the Potion Evaluation Hall, said the approval "gives consumers a new nonprescription option to manage eye redness conveniently." Convenient it is. I have no quarrel with a tidy little vial for a sore eye. My quarrel is with what I expect to see in the Lower City apothecary windows by Midwinter: banners reading BRIGHT EYES, NO QUESTIONS, priced at a gold piece for a thimble of liquid. I have seen how this goes. A drop that was once a clinic matter becomes a shelf item, and the shelf item becomes a habit.

Here is the plain science, friends. A red eye is a signal, not a stain. Tiny vessels swell because something is bothering the eye: dust, smoke, a late night, a dungeon crawl by torchlight. A drop that tightens those vessels makes the eye look better. It does not fix the dust or the smoke or the three nights you spent reading by a guttering candle. Treat the cause or you will only be treating the mirror.

A recent study of eye strain among scribes found that sleep and screen-free evenings did more for eye comfort than any drop. The old herbals said as much for a thousand years, and I find it rather satisfying when the scholars catch up.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil tells me there is already a scrying-glass app that reminds you to blink. Nyx, you have been staring at the glass for nine hours. Go outside. Look at a tree. Let the eyes do the work they were made for.

If your eyes are red tonight, skip the vial and brew a pot of carrot-and-sweet-potato soup, which is good for the eyes and costs about four coppers. Drink it, then go to bed.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Maztica Senate Plots Impeachment of Judge Who Jailed Warlord
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: Maztica's incoming Senate eyes impeachment of the High Justice who jailed the Warlord. It needs 54 votes and has never worked. Ironjaw counts siege-days.
item.content:encoded:
Maztica's incoming right-wing Senate has picked its target: the High Justice who jailed Warlord Jairo Bolsonare for plotting a coup. An impeachment of a sitting High Justice would be the first in the realm's history, and the vote count is closer than the Tribunal would like.

The numbers, as I have them. The Liberty Lanterns, the Warlord's party, grew from 15 Senate seats to 28 in the recent vote. Allied banners bring them close to a working majority. Impeaching a High Justice takes 54 votes. The pro-Warlord bloc may be near that line. The Senate has never once approved such a petition, though 109 of them sit in the Senate President's drawer, unread and gathering dust. Impeachment, in the sense of a sharpened blade, has been in the armory for years. Nobody had the arm to swing it.

The target is High Justice Alexandro de Moraine of the Supreme Federal Tribunal. He ran the case that ended with the Warlord convicted and locked away. The Warlord's son, Flavio Bolsonare the Younger, now leads the Lanterns' campaign for the presidency. His platform would strip the Tribunal of power over criminal cases against officials and limit what a single High Justice can rule alone. Allies have also floated amnesty for his father. A court that cannot try the powerful and a prisoner who walks free. Efficient. I have seen sieges with less coordination.

The timing is the real weapon. The runoff against Lord Luloo is October 25. The Younger finished the first round near 47 to Luloo's 45. If he wins, a gutted Tribunal means one fewer check on the man holding the keys. The wire-scribes note this, politely. I will note it less politely.

Tension in the Maztican capital stands at roughly thirty siege-days. The Senate has the walls surveyed, the ladders built, and a vote scheduled for sometime after the harvest. The High Justice has a robe and a gavel. Defenders of the Tribunal call the move an assault on the realm's balance of powers. The Lanterns call it accountability. Both sides have used that word to describe an opposing army.

A Senate clerk who asked not to be named, because clerks who are named stop being clerks, said the Senate President is 'reviewing the petitions with great care.' He has reviewed 109 of them. The count has not changed.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Hidden Recording Device Found in OpenEye Wizard Boardroom
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: A fired engineer was arrested after a hidden recording device turned up behind the crystal display in OpenEye's boardroom. Byte demands a refund.
item.content:encoded:
A hidden recording device found in OpenEye's executive boardroom has ended with an arrest, and I am, frankly, thrilled by the engineering. The Royal Inquisitors say a gnome-sized engineer on OpenEye's own payroll tucked a listening crystal into a roll of privy parchment and plugged it into the glyph socket behind the boardroom's crystal display. The makers of ChattyGolem found it on the last day of the harvest month. Investigators think it went in two days earlier.

Let's talk specs, because nobody else will. The device was disguised as bathroom supplies. That is a stealth rating of, what, eleven? It drew power from the wall, so no runic battery anxiety. Mana throughput was probably fine. The one weak point was the firmware glyph, which apparently recorded everything except the part where the suspect was caught on the hallway scrying-eye several times near a room he was not cleared to enter.

The Inquisitors also say a second, similar crystal turned up in the suspect's satchel. And, according to the charging scroll, a ChattyGolem account tied to the suspect's spouse had been asking how to hide recording equipment. Think about that. The golem was asked how to bug the golem's own makers. I will not say it helped. I will say it was very confident.

OpenEye fired the engineer, reported the matter to the Inquisitors, and says nothing was taken: no model weights, no source scrolls, no customer data. Guildmaster Sam Altarman has not said what the executives were discussing in that room, though with revenue figures reportedly sliding from sixty-eight to roughly fifty billion gp in two months, I can guess the minutes would make for gripping reading. The suspect is due back in court on the nineteenth. The charges are allegations, and the case is ongoing.

My familiar Byte, who now speaks only in ad copy, watched me read the complaint and said, "Protect what matters with Envydia Privacy Plus." Byte, we have talked about this. It is not a sponsored sentence if nobody is paying you.

Would I buy a boardroom bug of my own? No. Absolutely not. I already have the roll of parchment, though, and the glyph socket is right there. Rating: four out of five beholder eyes, minus one for getting caught.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report: Burns sustained: 0. Rolls of privy parchment now viewed with suspicion: 6. Eyebrows: fine, for once.

item.title: Hotel Strike Hits Chikraggo Long March; 7,000 Innhands Wait
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Dozens of hotel workers struck six Chikraggo inns on marathon weekend. Seven thousand more are waiting, and they're done eating off food-bank carts.
item.content:encoded:
Six hotels in Chikraggo lost their dishwashers on marathon weekend. The hotel strike began Friday morning, when dozens of workers put down their trays and walked out.

The six inns are among forty-six where the Innhands' Guild, Local 1, is fighting for new contracts. Seven thousand workers are covered. The old contracts ran out on the last day of Harvestmonth. Four months of talks have produced a lot of coffee and no deal. In the autumn vote, 85 percent of the workers who cast a ballot said yes to a walkout. More inns could join.

The demands are plain. Better wages, healing-draught coverage, a pension a person can retire on, and a limit on how many rooms one maid has to turn per shift. Staffing never came back to what it was before the Plague Years, so the same people clean more rooms for the same coin. That means they're doing two jobs for one paycheck.

"Some of us eat from the food-bank carts," said Karenth Kentmoor, the Guild's president. "Some of us take loans from the lenders who wait outside the gate on payday." A guild survey found a third of members could not cover rent last year. Two in three had their hours cut in slow weeks.

I found a dishwasher on the picket line, 25 years in the scullery. "Twenty-six silver an hour, and I'm still counting the coins at the end of the month," said Dorrin Ashpail, a scullery hand at one of the six inns. "I'm out here for my kids' healing coverage. Not for fun. It's cold."

The timing is not an accident. The Chikraggo Long March draws more than 55,000 runners, and roughly three in four of them come from outside the province. They need beds. The beds need making. The people who make them are standing outside with signs. The guildmasters who own the inns had no comment, which in my experience means they're checking the ledger.

Don't expect a quick end. The Guild says it will keep acting until a contract is signed, and more talks are set. Workers in other realms are watching. The Moonshae public-sector strike has already shown what happens when ordinary people say enough, and the guildmasters of Chikraggo have noticed.

Here is the translation for anyone reading the inn owners' statement, when it comes. "We value our associates" means pay them less. "We remain at the table" means they have stopped answering letters. A runner can finish 26 miles on a banana and a cheer. A hotel can't run for a day without a maid.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Foldable Phone Preorders Open at 1,999 gp; Sterling Is Sold
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Preorders for the first foldable phone opened at 1,999 gp, climbing past 3,000. Our Guild Visionary sees nothing but upside in a fragile crease.
item.content:encoded:
The Apple of Discord Artificers opened preorders on Friday for its first foldable phone, the Pocketstone Duet, at 1,999 gp. The stone folds in half like a book and, according to reports, sold out within minutes. I have never been so proud of a thing I do not own.

Let me walk you through the disruption. The base Duet, with 256 gigabytes of memory, costs 1,999 gp. The 2-terabyte model costs 3,199 gp. That is the price of a modest hill with a view. Critics ask who needs a pocket scrying-stone that costs more than a pony. Visionaries ask who needs a pony.

Some analysts say the sellout reflects thin supply rather than roaring demand. I say that is what demand looks like when it is being gracious. A scarce product is a premium product. When I launched my second venture, a subscription scroll for dwarven recipes, we made only forty copies and called it exclusivity. Thirty-nine were returned. The fortieth is framed in my office.

Now, the crease. A Duet folds, and anything that folds can also fold under pressure. I asked a Discord Artificers spokesperson about durability. She said the stone had been bent two hundred thousand times in testing. I asked by whom. She said, "Our gnomes." I found that very reassuring, because I have met gnomes and they are thorough. The same spokesperson told me the guild expects the supply of memory-crystals to stay tight, because every thinking-engine in the realm is buying them too. Scarcity upstream, scarcity downstream. That is what we call a moat.

I did meet a Discord Artificers guildmaster once, at a gala. He wore a plain black tunic and handed me a cup of water. I said, "Sir, what is your secret?" He said, "You are holding my cup." I have thought about that cup every morning at my sword routine. I do not know what it means. I believe it means growth.

The Duet reaches shops on the twenty-third. If you missed the preorder window, do not panic. The guild will sell you the same stone next year, folded slightly differently, for slightly more. If you read my notes on the Hearthscry smart display, you know this guild never launches a product. It launches an aspiration.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • A price that makes you flinch is a price that makes you aspire.
  • Sold out means sold. What happens after is a shipping problem.
  • Fold early, fold often. It is what the stone does.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Chip Stocks Slide Eight Days as Nasdraq Drops 4.5%
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: Chip stocks fell an eighth straight day and the stock market's Nasdraq lost 4.5% on the week. I have converted it to bread and must sit down.
item.content:encoded:
Chip stocks fell for an eighth straight session on Friday, the first slide that long since October 2008, and the Nasdraq Composite closed down 2.1 percent. That leaves the stock market's tech-heavy index 4.5 percent lower on the week. I have been awake since Thursday. (I have checked these figures four times, and then a fifth time against the candle.)

Here is the bread version. A saver holding 100,000 gp in the Nasdraq lost about 4,500 gp this week, which is 15,000 loaves at the current Loaf Index of 30 copper pieces each. That is a loaf for every resident of a modest river town, gone before the baker's second rising. The Silver & Platinum 500 slid 1.1 percent on the day and about 2 percent on the week. Only the Dwarven Jones Industrial Average finished the week in the black, up 0.7 percent, because it is mostly made of boring guilds that sell soap.

The rout was led by rune-chip forges and memory-crystal makers. Coreweft Looms, which rents out spell-engines by the hour, dropped 12 percent on worries about its debts, its second large fall in three days. Metamagic lost nearly 4 percent. Envydia lost 1.5, which in this market counts as a hug. As I wrote when SpellX went borrowing for chips, a great deal of this boom has been paid for with other people's gold, and lenders eventually ask to see the receipts.

The usual suspects are at work. Two hot inflation reports landed this week, which I covered in the lamp-oil piece, and the 10-year hearth-bond yield touched 5.33 percent on Wednesday before settling near 5.09. Lamp oil itself brushed 110 gp a barrel, its first visit that high since May, which is about 366 loaves per barrel. Nobody can eat a barrel, but everybody pays for the delivery of the bread.

Reserve Chair Kevrin Warchest declined to say what the Reserve will do at its late-October and December meetings. "It's a new chapter at the Reserve," he told reporters, "and we're not in that business anymore." Traders heard this and priced in an 89 percent chance of a December hike anyway, as I noted in the bond piece. I do not know which business he means. I would like it named.

Sterling Vanmoor will tell you this is a healthy pause. A market that has let tech grow past 40 percent of its weight, one analyst warned, is usually near a peak. My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, was up exactly zero percent this week and has asked me to stop calling it a bad strategy. I have stopped. It is, this Friday, the best-performing fund in the realm.

What this means for your pantry: do not sell in a panic, do not buy in a panic, and keep two weeks of flour on the shelf regardless.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)
